advances: Continuous Lebesgue densities with a specified convex inverse power. The statement concerns the maximum depth in one continuous space.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
Normalize $\int f=1$. The closure of the convex positive set is a full-dimensional compact convex support, and its interior belongs to the positive set. For a unit vector $u$ let $P(u,y)=\int_{\{x:u\cdot(x-y)\ge0\}}f(x)\,dx$. Moving any containing halfspace to have its boundary through $y$ only decreases its mass, so the depth is $\min_u P(u,y)$. Dominated convergence gives joint continuity because each limiting hyperplane is Lebesgue-null. Compactness of the unit sphere gives continuity of the minimum. This minimum is zero on and outside the support boundary by separation, and it is positive in the interior because the finite convex inverse power there is continuous and $f$ is bounded below on a small ball. Thus the maximum $\alpha$ is attained at an interior point $y_*$.

The active normals $A=\{u:P(u,y_*)=\alpha\}$ form a nonempty compact set with $0\in\operatorname{conv}A$. To prove the inclusion, suppose $u\cdot v\ge\delta>0$ on $A$ by strict separation. For the normals satisfying $u\cdot v>\delta/2$, moving the point to $y_*-\varepsilon v$ adds a slab of thickness at least $\varepsilon\delta/2$. Choose $R,m>0$ with $f\ge m$ on the radius-$R$ ball about $y_*$ and take $\varepsilon\|v\|\le R/2$. Every section of the slab in that ball has $(r-1)$-volume at least $\omega_{r-1}(R/2)^{r-1}$, where $\omega_j$ is the unit ball volume and $\omega_0=1$. The slab thus adds uniformly positive mass. The complementary compact set of normals has a uniform positive gap above $\alpha$ at $y_*$, and by joint continuity retains a positive gap for small $\varepsilon$. The resulting increase of depth is a contradiction. Carathéodory gives a finite subfamily of at most $r+1$ active normals with positive weights whose weighted sum is zero.

Apply the radial integral lemma with $p=r$ to $x\mapsto f(y_*+x)$. Dilating its body by $r^{1/r}$ gives a convex body $U$ with radial function
$$
\rho_U(u)^r=r\int_0^\infty f(y_*+tu)t^{r-1}\,dt.
$$
Polar integration gives $|U|=1$ and $|U\cap\{x:u\cdot x\ge0\}|=P(u,y_*)$ for every unit normal $u$. In particular the chosen active caps each have volume $\alpha$ in $U$. They cover $\mathbb R^r$, since at each point at least one of their scalar products is nonnegative by the positive balance. Thus every point of $U$ has depth at most $\alpha$, and zero has depth exactly $\alpha$ by the cap identities. The uniform-body lower bound in accepted fact 03bc771bddd39a8a applies to the full-dimensional compact convex body $U$ and gives a point of depth at least $\gamma_r|U|=\gamma_r$. Hence $\alpha\ge\gamma_r$. Finally the uniform density on a full-dimensional simplex satisfies the hypotheses, and its maximal normalized depth is $\gamma_r$ by the same accepted fact.
statement: Let $r\ge1$ be an integer. Let $f$ be a bounded nonnegative upper-semicontinuous density of compact support in $\mathbb R^r$. Assume $\{f>0\}$ has nonempty interior and the function $f^{-1/(r+1)}$, extended by $+\infty$ where $f=0$, is convex. Then there is a point $y$ in the interior of the support of $f$ such that every closed halfspace containing $y$ has $f$-mass at least $\gamma_r\int f$, where $\gamma_r=(r/(r+1))^r$. The constant is sharp.
title: Sharp halfspace depth for inverse-power-convex densities
